SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
 
I 
 
 The Committee takes note of the various amendments to the Rules carried out 
by the Ministry of Shipping, Road, Transport & Highways (Department of Road, 
Transport & Highways).  Its observations regarding some of these amend ments are 
indicated hereunder; 
(vii) Rule 1(3)  Rectifying the typographical error by deleting the words and 
figures ‘sub-rule 3 of rule 103’; 

 
(viii) Rule 4  Omitting  item No. 5 “ Electricity or telephone bill”  and item 
no. 7 “Pay slip issued by any office of the Ce ntral Government 
or State Government or  a local body” from the list of documents 
which can be treated as evidence for correctness of address and 
age for the purpose of issue of licence.   The Committee had 
suggested that identity card issued by the Central  or State 
Government can be included in the list of items that can be 
considered as evidence as to the correctness of the address and 
age of the applicant. Instead, the Ministry have deleted 
“Electricity and telephone bills as well  as pay slips of the 
Central/State Government in respect of their employees, in Rule 
4 as admissible evidence for proof of address and/or age.  The 
Committee notes that age and the address of the applicant for a 
driving licence are vital piece of information and therefore 
adequate care needs to be taken while making admissible 
evidence in support thereof.  Accordingly, items in rule 4 should 
be reviewed regularly to keep pace with the changing times but, 
additions/deletions therein should be done with abundant 
caution so that the provisions are not misused. 
 
(ix) Rule 5  Prescribing that an application for issue of learner’s licence or 
a driving licence or for making additions of another class or 
description of a motor vehicle to a driving licence or for renewal 
of driving licence to drive other than transport vehicle, must be 
accompanied by a self declaration as to the physical fitness  in 
Form 1 and an application for a licence to drive a transport 
vehicle must be accompanied by a medical certificate in Form 1-
A to be issued by a registered medical practitioner.  The 
Committee notes with satisfaction that by this amendment the 
provisions of rule 5 have been brought in conformity with 
Section 8 (3) of the Motor Vehicles Act whereby medical 
certificate is required only in case of transport vehicles; 

 
(x) Rule 7  Providing appropriate space in Form 1 -A for affixing of 
photograph in the Medical Certificate which was not there in 
the pre revised provisions; 
 
(xi) Rule 9  Substituting the words and figures “specified in the VII schedule 
of the constitution” with the words and figures “specified in the 
VIII schedule of the constitution” thereby rectifying the 
typographical error in Rule 9; 
 
(xii) Rule 50(1)   Substituting the existing Rule 50(1) by a new one giving 
specifications of the registration number plate in relation to the 
language, script as well as the kind of letters and numerals to be 
used therein which were not there in the pre-revised provisions;  
 
(vii) Rule 75(2)  Substituting the words “State Government shall” with the 
words “State Government shall, if so desired by the Central Government” so as 
to provide that the State Register of Motor Vehicles should mandatorily be sent 
by the State Governments to the Central Government whenever “desired by the 
Central Government”.  The Committee had questioned the periodicity of sending 
the State Register of Motor Vehicles maintained by each State to the Ministry of 
Shipping, Road Transport & Highways. The Committee, however, feels that the 
Central Ministry should have up-to-date data/records/information with regard to 
the Motor Vehicles in the States so that they have all relevant inputs and are able 
to formulate better and accurate policies, closer to the ground realities/needs in 
the field of transportation and motor vehicles. The Committee, in this c ontext, 
recommends that there should be a mechanism whereby the Ministry has access 
to relevant information/statistics at the State level on a regular basis. The 
Committee feel that computerization of relevant information at the State Level 
can be of great  help in this regard and the Central Ministry may take steps to 
ensure that the State Transport Departments computerize their records 
forthwith.  
 

(ix) Rule 89  The Committee notes with satisfaction that rule 89 has been 
omitted and accordingly, the inconsistency in the rule as pointed 
out by it has gone. 
 
 The Committee’s recommendations and observations arising out of the 
examination of the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 are enumerated below: 
 
(i) Educational qualification required  for issue of a driving license (Rule 9) 
 The Committee takes note of the fact that the existing provisions of the Motor 
Vehicle Rules 1989 do not prescribe any educational qualifications for procuring a 
driving license. Rule 9, however, pr escribes an educational qualification of a pass in 
tenth standard for obtaining a license for driving a goods carriage carrying goods of 
dangerous or hazardous nature to human life. The Committee is of the considered 
view that with the passage of time it h as become imminent that drivers of motor 
vehicles should possess some formal education so that they are able to read and 
understand various sign boards, directions etc. while driving. This is all the more 
essential in case of metro and big cities in the country where new and complex flyovers 
and relatively different traffic regulation are in force which may not be possible for 
an illiterate driver to understand or comprehend. The Committee does appreciate 
that prescribing a minimum education qualification c an adversely effect the 
livelihood of a sizeable section of people who are engaged in the business of driving 
but, equally important is the safety and security of the people around on the roads 
which is endangered due to the ignorance on account of illiter acy. The Committee 
feels that the safety of the road users outweighs and therefore recommends that the 
Government should consider to prescribe henceforth some minimum educational 
qualification say, 5th or 8th standard pass, for all types of licenses includ ing those for 
driving commercial vehicles. 
 
 As regards the requirement of a driving license for tractors when used as a 
transport vehicle, the Committee is happy to note that Government have taken up 
this matter with the State Governments. The Committee further appreciates that the 
Motor Vehicles Act prescribes a valid permit and other documents for use of a tractor 

as a transport vehicle. The Committee impresses upon the Ministry of Shipping, Road 
Transport and Highways to review the provisions of the Mot or Vehicles Act as well 
as the rules of 1989 framed thereunder so as to ensure that tractors, when used as a 
transport vehicle, whether for transporting goods or people, which is commonly done 
in the rural areas, does not remain unregulated and do not beco me a traffic hazard 
on the roads. The Committee accordingly recommends that Government may 
prescribe the requirement of a driving license subject to certain conditions keeping in 
view the rural background of the persons in case use of tractors outside the fields is 
to be allowed in order to maintain the safety and security of the road users. 
 
(ii) High Security Number Plates 
 The Committee is happy to note that Government are in the process of 
implementing high security registration plates for vehicles. The  Committee 
recommends that the Government should take up this project on priority and ensure 
that this is implemented within a definite timeframe. The Committee hopes that the 
implementation of this project would not only reduce instances of theft of vehicles but 
would also help in meeting the requirement of the law relating to the number plates 
i.e. the size and shape of the letters etc. 
 
(iii) Tinted Glasses 
 
 The Committee appreciates that tinted glasses on vehicles many a times 
become a hurdle for the security agencies in the prevention of crime and apprehension 
of criminals. But, the Committee would like the Ministry to keep in view the extremely 
hot conditions that prevail in most parts of the country during the summer period. 
The Committee feels that the requirements of security can be met in case light films 
are put on the vehicle which may not obstruct the visibility beyond the desired level. 
The Committee accordingly recommends that the Ministry of Surface Transport may 
work out on this issue with the security agencies for determining what percentage of 
visibility in a film would meet their requirement and the norms so determined can be 
notified for the information and compliance by the vehicle owners. The Committee 

would also appreciate if the manufacturers of such films are mandatorily required to 
indicate the percentage of visibility of the film on their rolls so that anybody who has 
put a film on his vehicle is confident that he is not violating the law. The Ministry may 
recommend similar action to the states also who may take action depending upon the 
climatic conditions and security requirements of their State. The Committee would 
also expect a definite policy of Government on this so that there is no uncertainty in 
the minds of the vehicle owners. 
 
(iv)  Use of Private Vehicles as Commercial 
 The Committee takes note of the various factors which prevent a vehicle owner 
to operate commercially on the basis of a valid permit namely, heavy taxation on 
commercial vehicles as compared to transport vehicles while entering from one state 
to another and even otherwise, procuring of fitness certificate for a commercial 
vehicle on a yearly basis as compared to a 15 year period for a transport vehicle, 
procuring of a permit for using a vehicle on commercial basis, etc. This vast difference 
between the requirements to be fulfilled in case of getting a vehicle registered for 
commercial or transport purpose and the financial implications involved in running 
a vehicle with a commercial permit is perhaps the main reason which prompts 
anybody to use his /her transport vehicle commercially. The Committee is unhappy 
to find such a state of affairs going on unendingly. The Committee is unhappy to find 
such a state of affairs going on unendingly. The Committee recommend s that the 
Ministry of SRT should consider this matter seriously as it not only involves revenues 
for the Government but also the safety and security of the commuters when vehicles 
operate unauthorizidely in the city or on the highways. Accordingly, the Co mmittee 
recommends that the Ministry should interact with the State Government on this 
issue in order to find out how such violations could be eliminated i.e. by rationalizing 
the financial implications so that the tendencies of violation are reduced. The 
Committee is conscious of the fact that violations in this area are a source of 
corruption with the implementing agencies and therefore, there is all the more a 
reason that a solution is found out and the sources of corruption are plugged once and 
for all. 
 

(v)  Better Regulation of Traffic and Enforcement of Traffic Laws 
 The Committee notes that the various traffic regulations under the Motor 
Vehicles Act are being enforced by the traffic police division of the State. Keeping in 
view the very heavy traffic that is seen on the roads in the big metropolitan cities 
(which is much more than the capacity of the roads) there is a need to make conscious 
efforts to see that the traffic moves in a regulated manner taking care of both the 
vehicle drivers a well as the enforcement agencies. The Committee is of the considered 
view that simply increasing the penalties cannot be a solution for instilling discipline 
among the vehicle drivers. In this context the Committee feels that the transport 
department of the State and the enforcement agencies i.e. the traffic police, can take 
some steps which may lead to disciplining the vehicle drivers on the roads voluntarily. 
For examples, both the state transport department and the traffic police can jointly 
or individually  consider educating the vehicle drivers on the traffic rules and 
regulations in a bigger way. This can be done by having some short programmes 
prepared and shown through the TV network as well as on the websites of the two 
departments. Secondly, the Committee feels that the traffic police in a city like Delhi 
should not give up its regulatory function of assisting and guiding the vehicle drivers 
at crossings and intersections which definitely is helpful and satisfying for the vehicle 
drivers. The Committee would also recommend that steps should be taken to device 
some specific training and refresher programmes for the traffic cops so that they can 
discharge their functions more accurately, responsibly and faithfully and eventually 
are able to win the confidence of the motor drivers. 
 
(vi)  Pollution under Control Certificate  
 The Committee is happy to note that a lot of attention is being paid 
particularly in big cities and metros to contain the menace of air pollution resulting 
from vehicles on road. There was an actual need for stern steps to check the high 
pollution levels caused due to emissions from vehicles in metropolitan cities where the 
vehicle population is too large. In order to keep the emission levels from the vehicles 
under check, the steps take n by Government with regard to bringing in higher in -
built technology in the vehicle and upgrading the quality of the fuel are laudable. But, 
the system of making all vehicles undergo a pollution check on a on -going basis calls 

for a review. In the first p lace, Government has not made any distinction between a 
commercial and a private vehicle for this purpose and anybody would agree that the 
commercial vehicles are put to use much more extensively as compared to private 
vehicles and therefore, the chances o f distortion of emissions are more in case of 
commercial vehicles as compared to the private vehicles. Secondly, the Motor 
Vehicles Act prescribes a validity period of 6 months for a PUC certificate i.e. a 
vehicle should undergo pollution check at least on ce in 6 months. But, some of the 
states like Delhi have prescribed a validity period of 3 months for a PUC certificate. 
Therefore, in a city like Delhi all vehicles are required to undergo a pollution check 
once in 3 months. It is doubtful whether the State of Delhi has enough paraphernalia/ 
infrastructure for the work of this magnitude and as a result, several vehicles continue 
without a PUC. Thirdly, the new vehicles with upgraded technology being used as 
private vehicles hardly go beyond the prescribed e mission norms. Even the new 
vehicles are required to get a fresh PUC certificate after three months of taking 
delivery. Keeping in view all these factors, the Committee recommends that the 
Government should review the existing dispensation so that people are not compelled 
to queue up for obtaining PUC certificate so frequently when their vehicles are well 
designed to adhere well to the prescribed emission norms. The Committee 
incidentally finds that in a city like Delhi, the job of issuing PUC certificates has been 
entrusted to private individuals who are located mostly at the filling stations. In this 
context the Committee recommends that an authorization can be given to the 
authorized service stations also for different brands of vehicles so that the vehic les 
undergo a pollution check along with each service. This would ensure an automatic 
pollution check of all vehicles at least once or twice a year without any extra effort on 
the part of the vehicle owners. 
(vii)  Certificate of Fitness     
 The Committee  notes that the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, and the Central 
Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989, do not prescribe any age limit for passenger buses and 
private vehicles. The only restriction is in terms of years for issue of National Permit 
for different types of vehicles. Similarly, the Supreme Court has not fixed the age of 
the vehicles but has put certain restrictions on registration/plying of commercial 
vehicles older than 8 years. Also, a certificate of fitness is issued in respect of new 
transport vehicles to be  valid for 2 years and to be renewed every three years. The 

Committee feels that the States lack in infrastructure for carrying out necessary 
periodic checks on the transport vehicles, whose number is too large. The Committee, 
however, is of the view that there is a need for stricter provisions so that the vehicles 
on road are better maintained and in good working condition, which would also 
enhance safety on road and reduce the number of accidents. Government may 
consider improving the infrastructure so that the checks on the vehicles are thorough 
and effective and eventually with improved infrastructure, private vehicles are also 
brought into this regime at least in the metro cities to being with. 
 
 The Committee hopes that the Ministry shall carry out necessary amendments 
expeditiously under intimation to it.   
 
II 
 The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry has carried out the 
amendments as suggested by the Committee on Rule 9(1) of the Prevention of Cruelty 
to Animals (Slaughter House) Rules, 2001 as contained in its 164th Report and decided 
not to pursue the matter further. 
 
III 
 
 The Committee notes with satisfaction that the Ministry of Finance (Banking 
Division) have taken necessary follow up action on its suggestions as follows :- 
 
 
(v) In Regulation 2 (g), by amending it so as to include legally adopted child in 
the definition of child so as to make the provision more liberal with regard to 
giving pensionery benefit to a legally adopted child  also. 
  
(vi) In Regulation 17, by notifying the amendments therein for counting the 
period of leave not exceeding twelve months granted on grounds such as 
sickness, higher studies and such other grounds as may be approved by the 
Board during the entire period of service for all purposes including pension in 

order to make the provision more specific about the reasons for granting such 
leave and  setting up the norms of sanctioning such leave. 
 
(vii) In Regulation 33, by notifying the amendments therein for making 
pension payable from November, 1, 1993 in case of employees who retired 
prior to that date and from the date of retirement in case of those who retired 
after that day so as to extend the pensionery benefit to the employees. 
 
(viii) In Regulation 35, by notifying the amendment th erein for raising the 
minimum amount of pension in lines with the recommendations made by the 
Committee thereby extending the financial benefit  to the employees of the 
Bank. 
 
 So far as Regulation 3 is concerned, the Committee decides not to pursue the 
matter as the interested employees have since  exercised their option and the issue has 
become redundant.  The Committee also accepts the Ministry’s view point on 
regulation 15  & 18 and decides not to press for changes in them any more. 
 
 With regard to Reg ulation 18,  the Ministry/Exim Bank has not taken any 
action stating that since the recommendations made by the Committee is on the lines 
of CCS (Pension) Rules and  this provision of Exim Bank under Pension Regulations 
are in line with that of Public Sector Banks and hence it has not been found possible 
to agree to the suggestions made by the Committee.  The Committee, however, was 
satisfied with the Ministry’s reply and it was decided to keep the provision as it is. 
 
IV 
 
 The Committee notes with satisfaction that the Ministry of Finance (Banking 
Division) have accepted some of its recommendations and has taken necessary action 
upon them as under: 
 
 •   Reg  2 (o):     By rephrasing the regulation 2 (o) as “son or unmarried 
daughter or widowed/divorced daug hter including such son or daughter 

adopted legally till he/she attains the age of 25 years or upto his/her 
marriage/re-marriage, whichever is earlier”, thereby making its provisions 
clear and unambiguous.  
•   Reg  8:       By agreeing to amend  the regul ation 8 so as to provide a fixed 
tenure of 3 years for the Board of Trustees to be eligible for reappointment, 
but may not be nominated for more than two tenures, thereby prescribing a 
term for the Board of Trustees. 
•   Reg 9:       By agreeing to amend the regulation 9 by specifying the purpose/ 
objective of the directions from the banks to the trustees, in order to minimize 
the scope for excessive or discretion by the banks. 
•   Reg  10:    By agreeing to arbitrarily  fixing a period of two months from the 
date of publication of balance sheet of the Bank for closure of the books of 
accounts of the Pension Fund, thereby reducing the prescribed 180 days to two 
months  for preparing the banks financial statement. 
  
 The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Finance should carry on the 
amendments in the  Regulations as above expeditiously.

Report item 
on 
Statutory Investigation into Railway Accident Rules, 1998- Implementation 
of the 138th Report of the Committee. 
 
 The Statutory Investigation into Railway Accident Rules, 1998 framed under 
the Railways Act, 1989 were examined and the Committee, in its 138 th Report 
presented to the House on the 14th March, 2002 recommended as under: 
 
“The Committee is unhappy to note that the Ministry of Civil Aviation 
are not aware of the correct legal position insofar as the requirement of laying 
of Rules in hand before the Parliament is concerned when they say that the 
Railways Act, 1989 does not specifical ly provide for laying of the Rules before 
Parliament. This is not factually correct. The Committee draws the attention of 
the Ministry to Section 199 of the Railways Act, 1989 which provides that all 
Rules framed under the Act shall be laid before each House of Parliament. The 
Ministry of Civil Aviation should have checked up the position thoroughly 
before responding to the Committee. The Committee expects the Ministry of 
Civil Aviation to be more careful in future while passing information to 
Parliamentary Committees. 
 
The Committee is not convinced with the comments furnished by the 
Ministry on the question of treating reports on Railway Accident as 
confidential. The Committee still holds the view that such Report should not be 

treated as confidential in a routine manner since in major accidents the public 
and Parliament are entitled to know of the causes and remedial action being 
taken. If necessary, a portion of a Report may be kept confidential for a period 
of time and that too for reasons to be recorded in writing. The Committee hopes 
that the Ministry realizes the need to be transparent in its functioning so that 
public trust is build up with regard to the efficiency and reliability of public 
services. The Committee trusts that the Ministry of Civil Aviation would review 
the position and make suitable amendment in the rule under intimation to it.” 
  
2. The Committee forwarded the relevant extracts of the 138 th Report to the 
Ministry of Civil Aviation for necessary action on the 1 st April, 2002. The Minis try 
furnished Action Taken Note on the recommendations of the Committee on the 15 th 
December, 2002. The observations / suggestions of the Committee as contained in the 
138th Report and the Action taken by the Ministry thereon are reproduced below: 
 
(i) Committee's observation / suggestion on laying provision 
 
The Committee is unhappy to note that the Ministry of Civil Aviation are not 
aware of the correct legal position insofar as the requirement of laying of Rules in 
hand before the Parliament is concerned  when they say that the Railways Act, 1989 
does not specifically provide for laying of the Rules before Parliament. This is not 
factually correct. The Committee draws the attention of the Ministry to Section 199 
of the Railways Act, 1989 which provides tha t all Rules framed under the Act shall 
be laid before each House of Parliament. The Ministry of Civil Aviation should have 
checked up the position thoroughly before responding to the Committee. The 
Committee expects the Ministry of Civil Aviation to be mor e careful in future while 
passing information to Parliamentary Committees. 
 
 Action taken by the Ministry (15.12.2002) 
 
The Ministry is in agreement with the points raised regarding laying of Rules before 
Parliament about Statutory Investigation into Railw ay Accident Rules, 1998, and regrets that Section 
199 of Railways Act, 1989 containing the provision of laying the Rules before Parliament had been 
missed inadvertently. 
 
(ii) Committee's observation / suggestion on Railway Accident 
Reports 
 
The Committee is not convinced with the comments furnished by the Ministry 
on the question of treating reports on Railway Accident as confidential. The 
Committee still holds the view that such Report should not be treated as confidential 
in a routine manner since in maj or accidents the public and Parliament are entitled 
to know of the causes and remedial action being taken. If necessary, a portion of a 
Report may be kept confidential for a period of time and that too for reasons to be 
recorded in writing. The Committee h opes that the Ministry realizes the need to be 
transparent in its functioning so that public trust is build up with regard to the 
efficiency and reliability of public services. The Committee trusts that the Ministry of 

Civil Aviation would review the posit ion and make suitable amendment in the rule 
under intimation to it. 
 
 Action taken by the Ministry (15.12.2002) 
 
As regards the question of treating reports on Railways Accident as 
confidential, the matter has been considered in this Ministry, and the Ministry agrees 
with the views expressed by the Committee. In fact, in case of air accidents enquiry 
reports are not treated as confidential, and are made public after their acceptance by 
the Government. It may  be mentioned that recently, when this Ministry was 
considering the recommendations of Railway Safety Review Committee, a similar 
view was taken as follows:-

4. Thereafter, the Ministry of Civil Aviation vide their communication dated the 
16th June, 2003 informed that Section 116 of the Railway Act, 1989 provides that the 
Commissioner of Railway Safety while conducting an inquiry shall be deemed to be a 
Civil Court for the purpose of Section 195 and Chapter XXVI of the Code of Criminal 
Procedure, 1973.  The Ministry of Civil Aviation is of the opin ion that by adding a 
new sub clause in Section 116 of the Railways Act, 1989 as follows, Commissioners 
could be provided desired immunity from being called as a witness in court of law in 
cases which arise from investigation done by them: 
 
 “The Commissioners while conducting an Inquiry shall be deemed to be a Civil 
Judge for the purpose of Section 121 of the Indian Evidence Act and the protection 
available under the above Section will be extended to the Inquiries conducted by 
them.” 
  
The Ministry of Railw ays were, accordingly, advised by the Civil Aviation 
Ministry  to carry out the suggested amendment to the Railway Act, 1989 and 
thereafter the Statutory Investigation into Railway Accidents Rules, 1998 would be 
amended to make it possible to publish Inqui ry Reports immediately after 
finalization. 
  
The Ministry of Civil Aviation, accordingly, requested that further time of 6 
months beyond 15th June, 2003 may kindly be given for sending the final reply.  The 
Ministry of Civil Aviation, accordingly, on the 2 4th November, 2003 stated that the  
Ministry of Railways turned down the suggested amendment in the Railways Act, 
1989 citing legal standpoint.  In the meantime, Ministry of Civil Aviation has taken 
certain decisions on 3.11.2003 on the publication of Accidents Inquiry Reports of the 
Commissioner of Railway Safety as an interim measure to restore public faith in the 
institution and to bring transparency in the system until immunity to the 
Commissioners of Railway Safety is made available to finally remove t he 
confidentiality of the Accident Inquiry Reports.  These decisions are as under:- 
 
 Henceforth all preliminary Reports of the railway accident shall be 
made public immediately. 
 The accident inquiry reports of the accidents occurred during 1999 -
2000 onwards in which Railway Board’s comments have been received 
shall be compiled in abstract form and published in six monthly 
periodicals starting from 1st January, 2004. 

 The above periodical shall be distributed to various authorities as per 
mailing list for the  distribution of Accidents Reports on publication 
besides uploading the same on Website also. 
 
5. The Committee considered the matter at its meeting held on the 25th February, 
2004.  The Committee noted that its suggestion to make public the report on railway 
accidents had been accepted by the Ministry of Civil Aviation. As the Ministry of 
Railway was also agreeable to the amendment of Section 116 of the Railways Act as 
this stage, the Committee decided to grant extension of ti me to the Ministry of Civil 
Aviation upto June 2004 for carrying out the necessary amendments. As a follow up 
to their action taken note, the Commission of Railway Safety published the 1 st issue 
of the compiled abstract of the Railway Accident Inquiry Reports. 
 
6. Thereafter, the Ministry of Civil Aviation again sought extension of time in the 
matter on two occasions, upto 30.6.2005 and 31.12.2005, respectively which were duly 
granted.  In response to their further request for extension of time upto the 30.6.2006, 
this Secretariat issued a D.O. letter to the Ministry seeking status of the amendment 
of Section 116 of the Railways Act, 1989 and the likely time by which the same would 
be carried out before their latest request for extension of time upto the 30th June, 2006 
was processed. Also views/comments on the amendment of the Railways Act was 
sought from the Ministry Railways. 
 
7. The Ministry of Civil Aviation on 22 nd May, 2006 replied that six monthly 
periodicals containing abstracts of finalized Accident  Inquiry Reports are being 
published and distributed regularly to various authorities.  Thus the cause of accident 
and the decision of the Government on the recommendations made by the 
Commission suggestion measures to prevent recurrence of similar accidents in future 
and for overall improvement in safety in railways is being made public through these 
periodicals.  These publications are being uploaded on the website of the Ministry of 
Civil Aviation, thus making them accessible to the general public.  The Ministry also 
stated that with the coming into force of the Right to Information Act, 2005, 
information regarding Commissioner of Railway Safety’s Reports on Railway 
Accident can be made available on case to case basis, as per the provisions of RTI Act, 
2005.  
 
 The Ministry of Railways vide their D.O. letter dated 9 th August, 2006 stated 
that they have obtained the opinion of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company 
Affairs and that the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs in detailed 
deliberations with Legal Adviser has opined that the proposed amendment in Section 
116 is not legally sustainable. 
 
8. The Committee noted the reply furnished by the Ministry of Railways  and 
accordingly asked them to furnish a copy of the legal advice tendered by the Ministry 
of Law, Justice and Company Affairs .  The Ministry of Railways furnished the same 
on the 26th May, 2008 which states that: 
 
 “This issue has been discussed with the Law Secretary in detail.  Legal Advisor 
(Railway) vide note dated 05.03.08 at page 81/N has stated that Ministry of Railways 
D.O. dated 09.08.2006 to the Rajya Sabha Secretariat (as Sl.no.76) is contrary to that 
advice tendered by the Ministry of Law and Justice. 

 
 The main issue before the Legal Adviser while tendering opinion at page 71/N 
dated 21.2.2006 pertains to amendment of Section 116 of the Railway Act, 1989 to 
provide legal immunity to Commissioner of Railway Safety from being called as 
witness in the Court of Law.  Opinion of Legal Adviser dated 21.2.2006 as well as legal 
advice tendered by the present Legal Adviser dated 05.03.2008 have again been 
perused.  The advice as tendered by the then Legal Adviser dated 21.2.2006 appears 
to be legally correct and he opined that legal immunity to Commissioner of Railway 
Safety from being called as witness in the Court of Law cannot be provided under the 
law.  Hence, the proposal put forward by the Safety Directorate “is not legally 
sustainable”.  Accordingly, Ministry of Railways (Railway Board) may take further 
necessary action.” 
 
  
9. The Committee, after considering the advice tendered by the Ministry of Law 
and Justice (Department of Legal Affairs) that legal immunity to Commissioner of 
Railway Safety from being called as witness in the Court of Law cannot be provided 
under the law, is satisfied with the advice and decided not to pursue the matter 
further.  
 
 
Report item 
on 
The Spices Grading and Marking Rules, 2005 
 
 The Spices Grading and Marking Rules, 2006  framed under the Agricultural 
Produce (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937 were examined and a questionnaire on the 
subject was referred to the Ministry of Agriculture (Department of Agriculture and 
Cooperation) for their comments / clarifications on the 28th June, 2006. The Ministry 
furnished their comments / clarifications on the 22 nd November, 2006.  The points 
raised by the Committee and the comments/clarifications furnished by the Ministry 
are reproduced below: 
 
(1) Point raised 
 
The Species Grading and Marking Rules, 2005 seem to have been framed in 
supersession of a number of rules pertaining to different spices, framed from time to 
time under the Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937. 
 

What is the background in which this consolidated set of rules have been 
enacted, the salient features of this new set of rules, vis-à-vis the earlier ones, and the 
objective sought to be achieved therefrom? 
 
Ministry’s reply 
 
 Background 
 
(i) These rules were framed and notified between 1962 and 1998.  The Spices 
Grading and Marking Rules, 2005 have bee n enacted as there are a number of 
changes in terms of technology/technique of sorting, drying, introduction of modern 
instruments to analyse active components that are responsible for quality of spices 
and introduction of stringent food safety parameters.  Promotion of export of spices 
and their competitiveness in the global market are also the factors that led to 
supersession of the earlier rules by this new rule. 
 
(ii) The limits of food safety parameters were not prescribed in the earlier rules 
which have been taken care of in the existing Spices Grading and Marking Rules, 
2005. 
 
Salient Features of this new set of rules:- 
 
1. Spices Grading & Marking Rules, 2005 are more stringent than old 
one. 
2. The limit of food safety parameters have been prescribed in the  new 
rules whereas it was not prescribed in the old one. 
3. New quality parameters like Curcuminoid content in Termeric, 
Capsaicinoid in Chillies, Piperine content in Black Pepper and increase 
in Volatile oil have been prescribed to avoid adulteration and 
assessment of the quality. 
4. The new standards prescribed in the Spices Grading & Marking Rules, 
2005 will take care of international and domestic grade standard 

requirements, so that they may become competitive in domestic as well 
as international markets. 
 
Objectives of the Spices Grading & Marking Rules 2005 are as follows: 
 
(1) To harmonize the parameters of grade standards and Food safety with ISO 
and CODEX Standards so as to facilitate competing in the global markets. 
(2) To include food safety parameter to meet the requirement of the 
International Market and Prevention of Food Adulteration for domestic 
market. 
(3) To protect the consumer from the adulteration by introducing new quality 
parameters. 
(4) To boost export of the Indian spices so that farmers may get remunerative 
prices for their produce. 
 
(2) Point Raised 
 
As per Rule 1(2), the Rules shall be applicable to the 11 specified spices.  Is the 
list of spices enumerated in Rule 1 (2) exhaustive and if not, which spices have 
been left out and why? 
 
Ministry’s reply 
 
The Spices Grading & Marking Rules, 2005 containing 11 Spices (whole and 
Powder) is not an exhaustive list of spices.  In first phase, the standards of 11 
Spices which are considered to be more important and having good marketing 
potential, have been harmonized with International Standards.  The standards of 
remaining spices namely Poppy seeds, Saffron, Garlic, Curry Powder, 
Compounded Asafoetida, Seedless Tamarind, Sundried Raw Mango Slices and 
Powder, Nut-meg, Tejpat, Clove, Caraway and Black caraway and Mixed masala 
that were notified under Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937, 
will be revised on the above pattern. 
 

(3) Point Raised  
 
In Rule 2, there is a reference to the General Grading and Markin g Rules, 
1988. What is the number of commodities for which specific Marking and Grading 
Rules have been framed (for example in case of spices in the instant case) and what 
is the justification for having such specific rules when the general Rules already 
exist. 
 
Ministry’s reply 
 
The Spices Grading & Marking Rules, 2005 contains only 11 spices (whole and 
powder).  The General Grading and Marking Rules, 1988 provide general 
principles of grading and marking to all the agricultural and allied commodities 
covered under the Agricultural Produce (Grading & Marking) Act, 1937.  The 
General Grading & Marking Rules, 1988 also prescribe provisions for 
grant/charges of Certificate of Authorisation (C.A.), issue of duplicate C.A, 
suspension or cancellation of C.A., app roval of chemist, provisions of grade 
designation marks, packing and marking, payment of charges and fees, 
Certification of Agmark grading (CAG), redressal of consumer grievances and 
complaints, power of entry into the premises, inspection and search, seiz ure, 
detention and disposal etc. and how to make an appeal mechanism. 
 
Whereas the Spices Grading and Marking Rules, 2005 prescribed grade 
standards in terms of physical and chemical parameters for each specific 
commodity separately.  These rules will be a dministered under the provision of 
the General Grading & Marking Rules, 1988. 
 
(4) Point Raised-Rule 5 Grade designation mark-  
 
The grade designation mark shall consist of “AGMARK Insignia” consisting 
of a design incorporating the certificate of authorization number, the word 
“AGMARK” name of commodity and grade designation resembling the design as 
set out in Schedule-XXIX. 

 
What is the number of quality control agencies and grading laboratories in 
existence in the country; the Ministry may furnish state-wise status in this regard.  
The Rules do not provide for inspection of such agencies and laboratories.  
Whether Government have any objection in providing for inspection of the 
agencies/laboratories, and also the frequency of such inspection and the rank/level 
of the officer-in-charge of such inspection in the rule itself? 
 
Ministry’s reply 
 
The Directorate of Marketing and Inspection with its 11 Regional Offices, 26 
Sub Offices, 16 Regional Laboratories spread all over the country and a Central  
Agmark Laboratory are responsible for monitoring the quality of agricultural 
produce “as quality control agencies”.  In addition, the Officers of the 27 
State/Union Territories have been delegated powers under General Grading and 
Marking Rules, 1988 for u ndertaking grading and marking of agricultural 
produce. 
 
At present, there are 74 Private Commercial Laboratories, 117 State Govt. 
Grading Laboratories, 7 Co -operative laboratories under existence providing 
analytical facilities to the AGMARK packers to gr ade and mark their produce 
under AGMARK. 
 
The State-wise status is enclosed separately as Annexure-I. 
 
Gazetted Technical Officers of the Directorate of Marketing and Inspection of 
and above the rank of Marketing Officer are authorized by the Agricultural 
Marketing Adviser, on his behalf, for inspection of these Laboratories and 
monitoring of methods of marking and labeling. 
 
(5) Point Raised Rule 6(1) Method of packing- 
 

Spices (whole and powder) shall be packed in gunny bags/jute bags, poly 
woven bags, poly p ouches, cloth bags or other suitable packages which shall be 
clean, sound, free from insects, fungal infestation and the packing material shall 
be as permitted under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 made 
under Section 23 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (37 of 1954). 
 
When the material to be used for packaging is required to be as per the 
Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 what is the justification for 
enumerating some packaging materials like gunny bags, jute bags, etc. in Rule 6.  
Further the words “clean, sound, free from insects…..,”in rule 6(1) are capable of 
varied interpretation.  Whether Government have any objection in making the 
provisions of Rule 6(1) more specific. 
 
Ministry’s reply 
 
The gunny b ags, jute bags, polywoven bags, poly pouches, cloth bags are 
traditional way of packing spices and condiments as per the prevalent trade 
practices.  Hence, these packing material has been prescribed in the Rule 6(1). 
 
The words clean, sound and free from insect mentioned in rule 6(1) also occur 
in National as well as International standards for maintaining high order of food 
hygiene and to increase shelf life and safeguarding the quality of the spices.  Hence, 
the word clean, sound and free insect mentioned in the Spices Grading & Marking 
Rules, 2005 are relevant words and admit no ambiguity and question of objection 
by the Government in making specific provision in the rule 6(1) does not arise. 
 
(6) Point Raised Rule 6(2) Method of packing- 
 
 Suitable lining of  food grade polypropylene/polyethylene/metallic shall be 
used for packing of Spices, (whole and powder) in gunny bags/jute bags, poly 
woven bags, cloth bags, paper bags and cardboard cartons. 
 

The word ‘suitable lining’ admit of varied interpretations.  Wh ether 
Government have any objection in substituting these words with appropriate 
words with certain specificities so as to make the provisions of the rules more 
specific? 
 
Ministry’s reply 
 
Scientific research and development took place from time to time i n the field 
of packaging material and suitable thickness of lining of food grade material is 
required for safeguarding the spices from moisture, fungal growth and safe 
transportation to maintain its own characteristics and quality. 
 
 
(7) Rule 6(3) Method of packing- 
 
Container and packaging material, shall be made of substances which are safe 
and suitable for their intended use.  They should not impart any toxic substance 
or undersirable odour or flavour to the product. 
 
Whether Government have any objection in specifying in the rule itself the 
substances with which the containers and packaging materials shall be made of 
for the purpose of the rule to make the rule specific. 
 
Ministry’s reply 
 
  The packaging material certified by the CFTRI, Mysore is allowed to be used

to improve the quality of the packaging material to increase the shelf life of the 
product and to protect quality, the change  in the parameter of the food grade 
packaging material take place from time to time.  Hence, it will not be appropriate 
to specify the same in the Spices Grading and Marking Rules, 2005 and objection 
from Government in specifying in the rule does not arise. 
 

(8) Point Raised Rule 7(1) & (4)- 
 
(1) A grade designation mark shall be securely affixed to or printed on each 
package in a manner approved by the Agricultural Marketing Adviser or 
an officer authorized by him in this behalf in accordance with Rule 11  of 
the General Grading and Marking Rules, 1988. 
(2) The authorized packer, may, after obtaining prior approval of the 
Agricultural Marketing Adviser or an officer authorized by him in this 
behalf, mark his private trade mark or trade brand on the graded 
packages provided that the same do not indicate quality other than that 
indicating by the grade designation mark affixed to the graded packages 
in accordance with these rules. 
Who may be the officer authorized by the Agricultural Marketing Adviser on 
his behalf for the purposes of the above rules?  Can the minimum level/rank of such 
‘officer’ not be specified in the rule itself? 
 
Ministry’s reply 
 
Gazetted Technical Officers of the Directorate of Marketing and Inspection of 
and above the rank of Marketing Officer are au thorized by the Agricultural 
Marketing Adviser, on his behalf, for monitoring methods of marking and labeling. 
 
The minimum level/rank of such ‘officer’ are not required to be specified in 
the rules itself. 
 
(9) Point Raised  Rule 8 (1) Special conditions of certificate of authorization- 
 
The authorized packer shall either set up his own laboratory or have approved 
grading laboratory for testing of Spices (whole and power). 
 
The rule gives option to the authorized packer to either set up his own laboratory 
or have access to an approved grading laboratory for testing of spices.  What about 

conditions governing the setting up of private laboratory and where these are 
specified? 
 
Ministry’s reply 
 
In respect of a commodity which require l aboratory testing for quality 
assessment, there is a provision under Rule 8 of General Grading and Marking Rules, 
1988 about setting up of own laboratory and approval  of State Grading Laboratory 
or Cooperative /Association Laboratory or a Private Commerci al Laboratory.  
According to Grading & Marking Rules, 1988 the authorized packer shall either set 
up his own laboratory or have access to an approved grading laboratory for testing 
of Spices (whole and powder).  The guidelines/instruction for setting up of  
laboratories is issued by an administrative order from time to time.  As these 
guidelines/instructions change from time to time as and when new parameters 
prescribed or new methodology of analysis of the parameters take place.  Hence, it 
will not be appro priate to specify in the Spices Grading & Marking Rules, 2005.  A 
list showing number of approved grading laboratories functioning in States and 
Union Territories has been placed at Annexure-I. 
 
(10) Point Raised Rule 8 (2) Special conditions of certificate of 
authorization- 
 
The premises shall be maintained in hygienic and sanitary conditions with 
proper ventilations and well lighted arrangement.  The personnel engaged in these 
operations shall be in sound health and free from any infections, contagious or 
communicable diseases. 
 
In what manner Government purposes to (i) implement the requirements of 
hygienic and sanitary conditions of the premises and (ii) ensure that personnel 
engaged in these operations are in sound health and free from any infectious, 
contagious or communicable diseases?  Whether Government have any objection in 
specifying the details in this regard in the rule itself? 
 

Ministry’s reply 
 
Provision of inspection of premises, hygienic and sanitary conditions with 
proper ventilation etc. are ens ured by issuing administrative instructions from time 
to time as per General Grading and Marking Rules, 1988 issued under section 3 of 
the Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937. 
 
The guidelines generally change from time to time in the inter est of 
safeguarding the shelf life and quality of the spices, maintaining good sanitary 
conditions and enhancing the quality.  Hence, it is not appropriate to specify the 
details in this regard in the Spices Grading and Marking Rules, 2005 and objection 
from Government in specifying in the rule does not arise. 
 
(11) Point Raised Rule 8(3)-  
 
The premises shall have adequate storage facilities with pucca floor and free 
from rodent and insect infestation. 
 
The word ‘adequate’ admit of varied interpretations.  Whether Government 
have any objection in substituting the word with some more appropriate words/phase 
so as to make the provision of rule 8(3) specific? 
 
Ministry’s reply 
 
The size of the storage depends on the capacity of the factory or machineries 
installed by the packer.  Therefore, the authorized packers have different size of 
storage facilities as per their requirements. 
 
Hence, the word ‘adequate’ is a suitable word and admit no ambiguity. 
 
2. Thereafter, the Committee took up the matter with the regi onal 
representatives of the Directorate of Marketing and Inspection alongwith the 
Ministry of Agriculture (Department of Agriculture and Cooperation) at 

Thiruvananthapuram on the 5 th January, 2007and a study note on the subject has 
been placed at Annexure II.  The Ministry of Agriculture (Department of Agriculture 
and Cooperation) vide their O.M. No. 18011/8/2002 -M.II(Pt) dated 1 st June, 2007 
have furnished their comments on the points that came up during the said visit 
(Annexure-III). 
 
3. The Committee not es that the Ministry of Agriculture (Department of 
Agriculture and Cooperation) is not in agreement with most of the suggestions raised 
by the Committee such as: 
 
(i) In Rule 5 to provide for inspection of the quality control 
agencies/grading laboratories, and also to specify the frequency of such 
inspection and the rank/level of the officer-in-charge of such inspection.  
(ii) In Rule 6 (1) to make the provisions more specific as the words “clean, 
sound, free from insects…” particularly the word “sound”, are capable 
of varied interpretation. 
(iii) In Rule 6 (2) to substitute the words “suitable lining” which admit of 
varied interpretation with more appropriate words so as to make the 
provisions of the rules more specific. 
(iv) In Rule 6 (3) to specify in the rule itself the sub stances with which the 
containers and packaging materials shall be made to make the rule 
specific. 
(v) In Rule 7 (1) & (4) to specify he minimum level/rank of the officer who 
may be authorized by the Agricultural Marketing Adviser on his behalf 
for the purpose of these rules. 
(vi) In Rule 8 (3) to substitute the words “adequate” which is subject to 
varied interpretations with some more appropriate word so as to make 
the provision specific. 
 
The Committee recommends that changes may be suitably incorporated in the 
Spices Grading and Marking Rules, 2005 in view of the above suggestions.  
 

The Committee expresses its unhappiness at the quality and purity of spices 
available particularly with the local sellers. The Committee observes tha t there is 
need for specifications to meet the international standards not only in respect of spices 
meant for export but also those for consumption in the domestic market. The 
Committee takes serious note of the reports of rampant adulteration of these items in 
the local markets. In view of this, the Committee strongly recommends that 
certification of spices should be made mandatory.  The Committee further observes 
that some items being sold under AGMARK license do not meet the desired quality 
and there is  fake imprint of AGMARK on items sold by the local sellers. The 
Committee therefore strongly recommends that the Ministry should take steps to 
ensure that specialized and technically advanced equipments are used while making 
AGMARK insignia so that it is i mpossible to replicate/forge it. The nodal Ministry 
should curb such malpractices and impose strong punitive measures. 
 
The Committee is concerned about the fact that India’s share in the world 
spice market is dwindling.  The Committee is of the view that while the price of spices 
in the international market are soaring our farmers are deprived of the profit. The 
Committee observes that the Ministry should disseminate the appropriate 
information to the farmers living in the countryside regarding prices, etc . The 
Committee observes that in the globalised market, Spices Board should devise 
mechanism to help farmers increase their productivity which is much lower in India 
than the world standard.

2. During the course of scrutiny of these Orders, the Committee has noted

In some of the cases the delay has been quite long. The 
observations/recommendations of the Co mmittee in respect of the specific 
Ministries/Departments are as follows: -    
  
(i) Ministry of Agriculture (Department of Agriculture & 
Cooperation) 
  
 The Ministry of Agriculture (Department of Agriculture & 
Cooperation) have laid 9 notifications out of whic h 5 (Sl. Nos. 1,2,5,6 and 8)

accompanied by any delay statements. Only  one notification has been attached

9 months. The reasons for delay given by the Ministry are as under: 

: 3 : 
 
 “The Notification G.S.R. 717 (E), dated the 15 th November, 2007  was 
published in the Gazette of India (Extra ordinary) Part-II, Section 3(i). The 
rules could not be laid down before each  House of Parliament in the Winter 
Session of Parliament as sufficient numbe r of copies of the Rules were not 
received in time from Government of India Press, New Delhi.” 
  
 The Committee notes with regret that  the Ministry of Agriculture 
have again failed to strictly adhere to the time schedule as prescribed in its 
131st Report that is reiterated as follows:- 
 
  “Orders required to be laid before  the House should be laid (i) if 
the House is not in Session, during the Session immediately following the 
date of publication of the Order in the Official Gazette and (ii) if the

Ministries/Departments of Governme nt of India should henceforth 
comply with this schedule in the matt er of laying of the Orders issued

 The Committee hopes that the Ministry of Agriculture would put

hopes that the Ministry of Agricultu re would be able to ensure that such 
delays do not recur in future.

 have laid 75 notification  on the Table of the

 The Committee urges the Ministry of Textiles to invariably

(xii) Ministry of Women and Child Development 
 
 Ministry of Women and Child Development have laid two

(ii) 

Report on the 
All India Institute of Medical Sciences Regulations, 1999 
 
 
After the independence of India in 1947, the founding fathers of the country 
visualized the setting up of a world -class institution in the field of medi cal education; 
research and patient care so that the doctors in the country could get the benefit of a 
high standard of medical education and research in the country itself instead of going 
abroad. Accordingly, the All India Institute of Medical Sciences ( AIIMS) was set up as 
an autonomous body under the All India Institute of Medical Sciences Act, 1956. Section 
13 of the AIIMS Act, 1956 outlines the objectives of the Institute as: 
 
a.       to develop patterns of teaching in under -graduate and post -graduate m edical 
education in all its branches so as to demonstrate a high standard of medical education 
to all medical colleges and other allied institutions in India; 
b.   to bring together in one place educational facilities of the highest order for the 
training of personnel in all important branches of health activity; and 
c  to attain self-sufficiency in post-graduate medical education. 
 
2. It was envisaged that there should not be any unwarranted bureaucratic/executive 
control in the day-to-day functioning of AIIMS.  In fact, the then Hon’ble Union Health 
Minister, Madam Raj Kumari Amrit Kaur while piloting the bill with regard to AIIMS 
in Lok Sabha on the 18th February 1956, had specifically stated:  
 
“Subject to such minimum control as the Government of India may ex ercise through its 
rule-making powers, the Institute will enjoy a large measure of autonomy in order that 
it may fulfill the objectives…The Government of India will, of course, make itself 
responsible for providing adequate funds for the maintenance of the institute…. 
The future of the Institute will lie ultimately in the hands of the Directors, the Professors 
and other members of the teaching staff and students…” 
 
3. The AIIMS Act, 1956 provides for framing of rules by the Central Government 
under Section 28 and framing of regulations by the Institute, with the previous approval 
of the Central Government, under Section 29. Accordingly, AIIMS, with the prior 
approval of the Central Government have framed the All India Institute of Medical 
Sciences Regulations, 1999.  
 

4. These Regulations were identified for examination by the Committee on Subordinate 
Legislation, Rajya Sabha in 1999 and the Committee had been in correspondence with 
both the Department of Health and AIIMS since then on various issues. During the 
course of its examination, the Committee took the oral evidence of  the representatives 
of the Department of Health and AIIMS, on the 27th September, 2001, the 28th January, 
2005, the 27th September, 2006 and the  29th March, 2007.  The main issues that cropped 
up during these exercise have been enumerated below:  
 
Delay in framing of regulations 
 
5. The Committee noted that although the AIIMS was set up under AIIMS Act, 1956 
the regulations contemplated thereunder were framed after about 43 years in 1999.  
When asked about the inordinate delay in the framing of the regulations and that how 
the AIIMS was regulated all these years in the absence of these regulations, the Ministry 
clarified that the first set of these regulations were formulated and approved by the  
Government on the 14th October, 1958.  The same had to be notified by publishing in the 
Official Gazette, but due to oversight AIIMS failed to do it, instead they had wrongly 
forwarded it to the Accountant General, Central Revenue.  Later on, although fou r 
amendments were carried out, but this discrepancy was not discovered.  It was only in 
1998, when the proposal to amend the regulations for increasing retirement age in 
compliance with the recommendations of the Fifth Pay Commission was sent to Law 
Ministry, this mistake came to the notice of the Ministry.  After discussions with the 
Ministry of Law a new set of regulations was notified in 1999 including all the 
regulations notified earlier, so that retrospectively they get regularized.  The Law 
Ministry felt that the past actions do not need any revalidation.  
 
6. The Committee is dismayed over recurrence and persistence of an oversight for 43 
long years despite the existence of Section 29 sub Section (3) in the Act which stipulates 
that the regulations framed under such Section should have been laid before each House 
of Parliament as soon as they are made. The Committee ho lds the Ministry responsible 
for such omission. As evident in the succeeding Para graphs of this Report, during the 
detailed examination of the AIIMS Act, 1956, the Committee gathered an unmistakable 
impression that the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare purposely and 
systematically abrogated the objective of the Act by retaining ambiguities in the 
Regulations.   
 

Regulation 4 (2) (b) of the AIIMS Regulations, 1999 regarding Minutes of the Meeting of 
the Institute Body 
 
7. The regulation reads as follows:- 
“All proceedings of the meetings of the Institute shall be entered in a Minutes Book to be 
maintained by the Secretary for the purpose and e ach minute shall be signed by the 
President of that meeting after the same is duly confirmed.” 
 
8. The sub-regulation is silent about the procedure regarding circulation of minutes to 
the members of the Institute particularly for the benefit of those members who could not 
attend the meeting on a particular day. The Committee queried whether the Ministry 
have any objection in incorporating such a provision in the regulation. 
 
9. The Committee also observed that the regulations regarding (a) calling of a meeting, 
(b) preparation of agenda, (c) procedures for circulation of minutes like who will record 
the minutes, who will circulate the minutes, whether the minutes to be circulated to the 
members for approval has to have prior approval of the chairman first, (d) the  time-
frame for circulating the minutes and seeking the approval from the members, (e) who 
will prepare the final draft of the approved minutes and finally (f) entering the minutes 
in the minute -book with due authentication by the signature of both the sec retary and 
the president/chairman are specious.  
 
10. Similarly, regulation 4 (9), that empowers President to include in the Agenda 
fresh/supplementary items, has been a controversial regulation for many years.  Often 
agenda items of far reaching importance are included at the last moment leaving no time 
for the members to participate in a meaningful and considered manner.  The Committee 
feels that it should be done in rarest of the rare cases and ordinarily, no important 
matter should be taken up without prior notice of all the members unless it is an urgent 
issue which has emerged after the meeting has been fixed and an Agenda has been 
circulated. 
 
11. With regulation 4 (2) a President has the power to decide the place, date and the time 
of the meeting.  All India  Institute of Sciences is situated in Delhi itself if the local 
situation is not favorable for which the reasons to be recorded then only meeting should 
be held at any other place, date and time as per convenience of the President. 
 

12. With respect to regulat ion 4 (11) the Institute is being run directly by the Director 
and he is responsible and accountable for its day -to-day affairs. So, which matter is 
urgent and/or important no one else except the Director is in a better position to decide. 
This decision sh ould not be left solely with either the President or the Government of 
India. 
 
13. The regulation is silent about fate of the members who often remained repeatedly 
absent in the meetings. There needs to be a clause for their removal, if they remain 
consistently absent in participating in the meetings without informing for more than 
twice. 
 
14. The Ministry vide its O.M. dated the 25th January 2000, informed that the minutes of 
the meeting were circulated to all the members as soon as the same was approved by the 
Chairman after the meeting, for inviting objections, if any. However, the Ministry said 
that it had no objection to the incorporation of such a provision in the Regulations. 
 
15. The Committee in its communication to the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare 
dated the 13th June, 2003, enquired about action the Ministry had taken in this regard. 
The Ministry replied that the existing procedure regarding circulation of minutes had 
the approval of the Ministry and that the directions of the Committee on Subordinate 
Legislation, Rajya Sabha were being followed. However, a proposal for necessary 
amendment to this effect was under process for approval of the Institute Body. 
 
16. The Committee takes note of the Ministry’s response to the questionnaire vide its 
OM dated August 2008 wherein it was stated that proposed amendments to  the 
Regulations pertaining to the circulation of minutes had  not been placed before the 
Institute Body/ Governing Body. However, some three months have already lapsed since 
then and the Committee considers that the Institute /Governing Body should have taken 
a positive view of the proposed amendments during the interregnum. The Committee is 
of the opinion that Regulations must clearly fix the periodicity of the meetings of 
Governing Body and the Instit ute Body. The Committee feels that instead of leaving the 
decision on the President/ Chairman, at least one meeting of these bodies  should be held  
every quarter. The Verbatim records of the meetings should be kept along with the final 
minutes.  The Commit tee also recommends that the Draft minutes of the meetings of 
IB/GB should be circulated under the signature of the Director of the Institute and only 
the final minutes  duly confirmed by the members present, should be signed by the 

President and filed in the Minutes Book. Minutes may be circulated and confirmed by 
the Members electronically. 
 
Regulation 4(9) P owers  of the President to include fresh/supplementary items in the 
agenda for the meeting 
 
17. As regards Regulation 4(9) that empowers the President to  include 
fresh/supplementary items, the Committee recommends that any issue so included by 
the President or with his approval should be first adopted by the simple majority of 
members present and any decision thereon should be taken with 2/3 majority of th e 
membership of I nstitute. Similar practice should be adopted in respect of Regulation 
8(9) with respect of Governing Body with an exception that all the decision should be 
unanimous.  The Committee recommends that necessary provisions should be 
incorporated in the relevant Regulations.  
 
Regulation 4 (6)- Time period for calling extraordinary meeting 
 
18. The sub -regulation provides that an extraordinary meeting of the Institute can be 
called if at least nine members of the Institute desired so in writing. The  Committee 
wanted to know the justification for calling the meeting within one month and not at a 
shorter notice, especially when the notice period for calling an extraordinary meeting by 
the President was seven days, and for an ordinary meeting the notice  period was two 
weeks. 
 
19. The Ministry vide their O.M. dated the 25 th January, 2000, replied that the 
regulation provided for calling of an extraordinary meeting of the Institute within a 
period of seven days. Hence, the meeting may be called within a period  of 7 days or a 
fortnight but not later than one month. 
 
20. The Committee  further inquired that when there is a provision for calling an 
extraordinary meeting by President in seven days, why regulation 4(6) should also not 
provide for a period of ‘seven days’ for calling an extraordinary meeting of the  Institute 
instead of one month. The Ministry replied that normally, the meetings of the Institute 
Body or the Governing Body are called at the convenience of the President of the 
Institute. In case of urgency, the President can call an extraordinary meeting of the 
Institute Body/Governing Body for which a notice of seven days would be sufficient. The 

Ministry replied that the existing provisions are adequate for providing a notice period 
of one month in case of written request of 9 members of the Institute. However, it was 
assured by the Ministry that the views of the Committee would be placed before the 
Institute/Governing Body for their consideration. 
 
21. A proposal to have amendment in AIIMS Regulations, 1999 as suggested by the 
Committee was placed before the Governing Body in its meeting held on 3.4.2002. The 
Institute Body also concurred with the decision of the Governing Body in its meeting 
held on 11.9.2002. The Ministry of Health & Family Welfare has approve d the said 
amendment and this amendment has been carried out in the AIIMS Regulation, 1999, in 
regulation 4 (6) as under:- 
 
“An extraordinary meeting of the Institute may be called on a written request of  not 
less than 9 members of the Institute within 7 days of the receipt of the requisition and 
the request made by members for a requisitioned meeting shall indicate the purpose of 
the meeting.” 
 
22. The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry has carried out  the amendments 
suggested by it, incorporating t he provision that an extraordinary meeting of the 
Institute can be called on a written request of not less than 9 members of the Institute 
within 7 days of the receipt of the requisition vide regulation 4 (6) of the AIIMS 
Regulations, 1999. The Committee recommends that relevant background papers on the 
issue of such extraordinary meeting must be electronically or otherwise circulated 
among the members at least 5 days in advance. The relevant regulation must be 
amended accordingly.  
 
Regulation 4 (14) Confi rmation of business transacted through circulation of papers -
incorporation of savings clause 
 
23. This sub -section prescribes that the business of the Institute may be transacted by 
circulating paper and acted upon, if approved unanimously.  The resolution and  action 
taken thereon shall be placed before the meeting for confirmation.  The Committee felt 
that in case the resolution in this regard failed to acquire the confirmation there had to 
be a savings clause validating the things done in pursuance of the dec ision arrived at by 
circulating papers.  The Ministry in their reply dated 25 th January 2000, said that if the 
resolution had been unanimously approved by the members by circulation, the same 

was expected to be confirmed in the regular meeting, since the s ame members who had 
unanimously approved by circulation, will be present in the regular meetings also.  
 
24. The Committee reiterated its stand that there is nothing wrong in inserting a saving 
clause in regulation 4 (14), for saving any action taken in pursua nce of business 
transacted by circulating papers.  The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare vide their 
communication dated the 20th February, 2002 informed that the suggestions given by the 
Committee were noted and AIIMS was being asked to put up an agend a item for that 
purpose for the approval of the Governing Body/Institute Body.   The Ministry on the 
27th June 2005, informed that a proposal to have an amendment in AIIMS Regulations, 
1999, as suggested by the Committee, will be placed before the Institut e Body for 
approval. 
 
25. The Committee takes note of the Ministry’s response to the questionnaire vide its 
OM dated August 2008 wherein it was stated that proposed amendments to the 
Regulations pertaining the insertion of saving clause had  not been placed be fore the 
Institute Body/ Governing Body. However, three months have already lapsed since then 
and the Committee considers that the I nstitute/Governing Body should have taken a 
positive view of the proposed amendments during the interregnum.  The Committee 
strongly recommends that there must be inserted a saving clause in regulation 4 (14) for 
saving any action taken in pursuance of business transacted by circulating the papers 
and accordingly, AIIMS Regulations, 1999 , be suitably amended and a proposal to th at 
effect be approved by the Institute Body at the earliest. 
 
Regulation 18-Revision of fee for various courses 
 
26. The regulation provides for the fee payable for the Post Graduate and Under 
Graduate courses at the AIIMS.   The Committee found that the fees f or courses 
conducted at AIIMS were highly subsidized and wanted to know the justification for 
prescribing such subsidized rates of fee.  The Ministry vide their OM dated the 25 th

the Governing Body. 
 

27. When asked about the reason for keeping in abeyance the implementation of the

Committee decided that enhancement of tuition fee will be made appl icable to the

on 5.6.1998/17.61998. The Governing Body, after taking into consideration all aspects of

28. The Committee ta kes note of the Ministry’s response to the questionnaire vide its 
OM dated August 2008 wherein it was stated that  issues pertaining to revision of fee 
have yet not been taken up by the Institute.  The Committee expresses its concern about 
the intermi nable delay in rationalizing  fee struct ure in AIIMS . The Committee wants 
further clarification on the issue as to why the matter of rationalizing fee structure has 
been  pending for such a long time and if any further developments have taken place the 
Committee should be informed about it.  The Committee of the view that fee structure 
should be realistic and rational. The fee structure should be reviewed periodically after
